working.formula: 0.8 × breaker rating (the breaker is 125% of a continuous load)
working.name: Continuous current limit
working.reference: NEC 210.20(A) continuous loads at 125%, as applied by L&L; electric-and-thermal.md §3 [S25]

working.formula: P = V·I
working.name: Power the circuit can supply

working.formula: 20 A up to 13.3 A; above that, 150 % of the kiln's current, or the next standard size up
working.name: Largest breaker allowed
working.reference: NEC 422.11(E), a single non-motor appliance, as reported; standard sizes 240.6(A); electric-and-thermal.md §3 [S23, S79]

working.formula: ρ_T = ρ20 · Ct
working.name: Wire resistivity when hot
working.note: The wire is assumed to run 100 °C above the kiln; Ct changes little there.
working.reference: electric-and-thermal.md §1.1, §1.2, §1.4: Kanthal APM data sheet [S2], atmospheres [S9]

working.formula: d³ = 4·ρ_T·P² / (π²·U²·p)
working.name: Smallest wire for the surface-load limit
working.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.254 and p.257: 5–9 W/in² for normal electric kilns, 6.4–9 for cone 10; Kanthal's A-1 chart, p.253

working.name: Wire chosen
working.note: The fewest elements that work, then the thickest standard gauge (ASTM B258) for them: at or above the smallest diameter, with a coil that fits the groove at a pitch of 2–4 wire diameters. Thicker wire lasts longer (Kanthal).
working.reference: electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S9, S13]

working.formula: L = U²/P · (πd²/4) / ρ_T
working.name: Wire length per element
working.reference: Kanthal element design: R = U²/P, L = R·q/ρ_T; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S13]

working.formula: p = P / (π·d·L)
working.name: Surface load
working.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.254 and p.257: 5–9 W/in² for normal electric kilns, 6.4–9 for cone 10; Kanthal's A-1 chart, p.253

working.formula: turns = L / (π·(D − d)); pitch = groove length / turns

inputs.pitch range: at least 2 d in grooves (Kanthal key data [S14]), at most 4 d (Kanthal, general [S13])

working.name: Coil
working.reference: Kanthal, element in grooves; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S13, S14]

working.formula: installed power ÷ inside area of the element walls
working.name: Wall loading
working.note: Kanthal gives no figure above 1000 °C, where it can only be lower; and the floor and roof carry no elements here.
working.reference: Kanthal key data, spiral in grooves; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S14]

working.name: Installed power per unit of chamber volume
working.note: For comparison, 7 cu ft cone 10 kilns from L&L and Skutt have about 1650–1720 W/ft³ (electric-and-thermal.md §7 [S73, S74]).

working.formula: P_installed / Q_loss
working.name: Installed power over steady loss at top temperature
working.note: Power above the loss is what heats the ware and walls near the top.

At $0.12/kWh and $3.50/gal, electricity is the cheaper heat at every temperature, so run the elements as long as they can keep the schedule, and add the burners alongside them rather than instead of them.

findings.message: Cost per firing needs a firing schedule and the heat stored in the walls and ware; that comes with the firing simulation (plan milestone M6).

The heated thrust is worked out from statics. HarbisonWalker's table, which it matches to 4 %, covers T/S 4–10 % and 1–3 in/ft; this arch, at 10.7 % and 1.61 in/ft, is past it, where the same statics carry on.
findings.reference: statics with hinges at the arch faces (Heyman, maximum thrust); arch-thrust-theory.md [A1–A3], checked against HarbisonWalker's heated-arch table, kiln-hardware.md §4.3 [S20]

findings.message: Weld the frame and fit it before the arch form comes out: the steel is what holds the arch up.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §4.1–4.2 [S11] [S21]

findings.message: The front wall is the door: bricked up, dry, for each firing. Lay the inner and outer courses together, staggered, with a header course two-thirds of the way up.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §6.1 [S4]

findings.message: Side-mounted burners need a bag wall so the flames don't hit the ware: hard brick, first course solid in front of the burners.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §1.3 [S4]

findings.message: Damper: a kiln shelf in a slot 12 in wide and one course high, about a foot above the top of the flue. Brace the chimney with angle at its corners and tie it to the kiln frame.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §3.2–3.3 [S4]

findings.message: Three spy holes, 2¼ × 2½ in (a quarter brick), in the door: about 8 in above the floor (a course above any burner ports there), midway and near the top, a few inches off centre so they miss the shelf posts. Cone packs in the top and bottom, draw rings in the middle.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §2 [S4] [S13]

findings.message: Arch bricks: Back wall, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Door, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Left wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle; Right wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle.
findings.reference: Arch and wedge shapes, 9-inch series; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]

findings.message: The skewbacks and the fill beside the arch are drawn along the arch's radius at the springline and counted by volume. The skewback's face must match the arch: 60° to the horizontal here, 90° less half the arch's central angle (HarbisonWalker's 60° skews suit a 60° arch, its 48° skews one at 2.302 in/ft). The steel that takes the arch's thrust is in the frame.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §5.2 [S20]

findings.message: HarbisonWalker, for industrial furnaces: "A stretcher course should never be used immediately below the skewback." Brick in these side walls is laid as stretchers, as in Olsen's insulating-brick kilns, whose featheredge skewbacks sit on a stretcher hot face (p.176, p.140). Where you can, lay the course under each skewback as headers.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §4.1 [S20]; Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.176

findings.message: Castable: cure 16–24 h above 60 °F kept damp, never let it freeze, and dry it out slowly before the first firing (for Mizzou: 75 °F/h with a ½ h hold per inch at 250, 500 and 1000 °F). Follow the maker's sheet for your castable.
findings.reference: combustion-and-masonry.md §6.2 [S54, S56]

findings.message: Brick counts assume dry joints at the nominal 9 × 4½ × 2½ in size, a ⅛ in saw cut, and 10% extra for breakage. At the corners the side walls run through and the back and door fit between them, layer by layer.
findings.reference: 9 × 4½ × 2½ in straight; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]

findings.message: Arch bricks: Back wall, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Door, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Left wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle; Right wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle.
findings.reference: Arch and wedge shapes, 9-inch series; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]

findings.message: The skewbacks and the fill beside the arch are drawn along the arch's radius at the springline and counted by volume. The skewback's face must match the arch: 60° to the horizontal here, 90° less half the arch's central angle (HarbisonWalker's 60° skews suit a 60° arch, its 48° skews one at 2.302 in/ft). The steel that takes the arch's thrust is in the frame.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §5.2 [S20]

findings.message: HarbisonWalker, for industrial furnaces: "A stretcher course should never be used immediately below the skewback." Brick in these side walls is laid as stretchers, as in Olsen's insulating-brick kilns, whose featheredge skewbacks sit on a stretcher hot face (p.176, p.140). Where you can, lay the course under each skewback as headers.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §4.1 [S20]; Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.176

findings.message: Castable: cure 16–24 h above 60 °F kept damp, never let it freeze, and dry it out slowly before the first firing (for Mizzou: 75 °F/h with a ½ h hold per inch at 250, 500 and 1000 °F). Follow the maker's sheet for your castable.
findings.reference: combustion-and-masonry.md §6.2 [S54, S56]

findings.message: Brick counts assume dry joints at the nominal 9 × 4½ × 2½ in size, a ⅛ in saw cut, and 10% extra for breakage. At the corners the side walls run through and the back and door fit between them, layer by layer.
findings.reference: 9 × 4½ × 2½ in straight; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]
